interactions.summary: A student says there can be true counselors as well as false ones, but Jiang immediately turns the idea back on himself with a comic question about whether his own YouTube wisdom could get him to heaven, then answers no.
A remote question suggests the danger of celebrity is that followers stop using their own imagination, but Jiang insists that even genuinely educative influence would still not by itself save him.

One student jokes Jiang would share the fate of revered intellectual giants in Limbo, and another answers more seriously that heaven remains a personal journey of self-improvement and reflection even if one also happens to be a celebrity.
Jiang presses for practical advice about getting to heaven faster, and a student answers that heaven, purgatory, and hell begin only after a life's journey is complete.

speaker_notes.note: The comment is relayed from 'Jimmy,' so this segment is effectively a mediated remote audience question rather than a direct in-room student speech.

claims.claim: A student proposes that fame is not inherently damning because there can be true counselors as well as false ones.
Jiang answers his own test case negatively: even if his YouTube channel spreads wisdom, public influence is not what gets a soul from Purgatory to heaven.
The remote question suggests that celebrity can be spiritually dangerous even when the message is right because followers may surrender their own imaginative judgment and simply obey the idol.
A student argues that the journey to heaven is fundamentally personal, grounded in self-improvement and self-reflection rather than in public recognition.
Another student adds that the afterlife journey only begins once a person's earthly life is complete, so there is no literal acceleration while one is still alive.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang uses himself as the test case for sanctified celebrity and then denies that even wisdom-broadcasting fame saves.
signature_moments.source_phrase: i have my own youtube channel and i'm spreading wisdom
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps the lecture from staying abstract and lets Jiang expose the limit of public influence in salvific terms.

signature_moments.moment: The remote audience frames celebrity as a threat to imagination itself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: people will blindly follow what they say and not use their own imaginations
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharpens the critique of fame from pride to the deformation of the follower's soul.

signature_moments.moment: A student jokingly assigns Jiang to Limbo with the great intellectual giants.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It dramatizes the difference between admired intellect and salvific transformation.

signature_moments.moment: Heaven is recast as a fundamentally personal journey of self-improvement and self-reflection.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the journey to heaven is still personal fundamentally
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the packet its clearest positive answer to the fame problem.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The student's category for a respected public guide whose fame would not be fraudulent in the way false counselors are.
The remote question's warning that celebrity can short-circuit imaginative or moral agency in followers.
The student's counter to fame: ascent is finally individual work of reflection and improvement, not a reward for public status.

chronology_notes.note: The packet continues the celebrity debate by testing increasingly practical cases, from true counselors and Jiang's own channel to the stricter answer that heaven is a personal posthumous journey rather than a prize attached to influence.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's self-appraisal is partly comic, but the stable doctrinal point is that even beneficial teaching does not itself move a soul into heaven.
